headline: Maine child-development contracts put long-running USM program at risk
dek: DHHS conditionally selected New York-based Shine Early Learning for two contracts worth an estimated $10 million, a decision that could end the University of Southern Maine's decades-long role supporting child-care providers.
body: Maine has conditionally selected an out-of-state company to take over two child-development support contracts, putting the future of Maine Roads to Quality at the University of Southern Maine in doubt and raising questions about how the state will deliver training and technical help to early-childhood providers.

The Department of Health and Human Services offered the contracts to Shine Early Learning, a New York-based company whose work includes services for child-care centers, home-based providers and public schools in more than 30 states. The two awards are estimated at about $10 million over two years, according to [CentralMaine.com and the Portland Press Herald](https://www.centralmaine.com/2026/10/01/maine-dhhs-awards-child-development-grant-to-out-of-state-private-equity-backed-firm/). DHHS spokesperson Lindsay Hammes told the newspapers that the awards remain conditional and that the final value will be public after the contracts are completed; no contracts had been ratified when the report was published.

One contract covers coaching, credentialing and training for early-childhood educators and care providers. The other would provide a DHHS-approved training plan intended to improve the quality of child-care services and the educators who provide them. Those functions have been housed under one contract for much of the program's history, according to Samantha Warren, a University of Maine System spokesperson quoted by CentralMaine.com.

Maine Roads to Quality was created in 1999 through the Catherine Cutler Institute at USM. The program provides professional development and assistance to more than 10,000 Maine child-care providers each year, the newspaper reported. A [University of Maine program description](https://ccids.umaine.edu/research-projects/mrtq-pdn/) says the broader professional-development network also supports a child-care database, specialized training, inclusion consultation and a warm line for providers seeking advice. The university page identifies the network's funding as a Maine DHHS Office of Child and Family Services block grant.

That infrastructure is tied to how Maine evaluates and supports child-care quality. The [Maine DHHS description of Rising Stars for ME](https://www11.maine.gov/dhhs/ocfs/support-for-families/child-care/qris) says the quality-rating system is funded by the federal Child Care and Development Fund and administered by the department's Office of Child and Family Services. The Maine Department of Education says public-preschool staff must join the Maine Roads to Quality Registry and describes the network as providing free or low-cost training in person, online and in hybrid formats. A change in the operator therefore affects more than a single university program; it touches a statewide system that providers use for professional development and quality-rating work.

The competing proposals received sharply different scores. Shine's bid earned 97 out of 100 for the coaching contract and a perfect score for the training-plan contract, while Maine Roads received about 73 points on each proposal, CentralMaine.com reported. The state said the scores followed the process in its requests for proposals but did not explain the difference in detail. The newspaper also reported that Shine's proposals were about $2 million lower across the two contracts, though DHHS has not published the final contract values because the awards are not complete.

Shine's applications propose using artificial intelligence in several parts of the work, including a family-navigation assistant, an employee-vetting tool and an agent to manage a provider registry, according to the report. Those are plans in the company's applications, not evidence that the tools have been deployed in Maine or that they will replace particular services. The contracts also require Shine to employ at least 10 people in Maine, a staffing condition that leaves open how much of the current locally based support model would continue.

Maine Roads employs more than 30 people, and the University of Maine System said layoffs are expected if the DHHS contracts are not renewed. The system told CentralMaine.com that it plans to continue providing services through the end of the current contract and support employees who may be affected. It also plans to appeal the decision. For providers, the immediate issue is continuity: the state has announced a conditional selection, but it has not yet published a completed agreement or a transition schedule that explains when Shine would assume the work.

The next checkpoint is the contract process itself. DHHS will have to finalize the awards, disclose the completed values and set the terms for staffing, training, data systems and provider support. Until that happens, the selection signals a possible change in who administers a core piece of Maine's early-childhood infrastructure, but it does not by itself close Maine Roads to Quality or establish exactly how services will look under the proposed new operator.

seoTitle: Maine child-development contracts put USM program at risk
seoDescription: Conditional DHHS awards to Shine Early Learning could end USM's decades-long Maine Roads to Quality role supporting child-care providers.
